note: Draft: the first ten definitions supplied by Pradyum in the team chat. This is not the complete proposed list of forty or an approved final taxonomy. Review definitions before labeling; bump anchor_version when their meaning changes.

anchors.name: Eastern Front attrition and logistics
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about the grinding, resource-draining nature of the German-Soviet war (1941-45), such as manpower losses, supply lines, distance and weather, and industrial replacement capacity, rather than the tactical narrative of a single battle. Siege or encirclement operations count only if the passage focuses on their attritional or logistical effect.

anchors.name: Siege and encirclement warfare
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about large-scale sieges and encirclement campaigns on any front of the war, typically involving hundreds of thousands of troops and ending in mass casualties or the capture of large numbers of soldiers and prisoners of war.

anchors.name: Pacific island and amphibious campaigns
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about military campaigns in the Pacific theater (1941-45), whether Japan’s offensive conquests or the U.S. island-hopping advance, in which forces took territory by amphibious assault or defended it against one.

anchors.name: Battle of the Atlantic and convoy warfare
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about the naval struggle (1939-45) over Allied shipping across the Atlantic, in which German U-boats and surface raiders attacked merchant convoys carrying supplies to Britain and the Soviet Union, and Allied navies, merchant crews, and aircraft worked to protect them.

anchors.name: Strategic bombing as an operational campaign
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about sustained air campaigns against enemy cities, industry, and infrastructure (1939-45), such as the Blitz, the Allied bombing of Germany, and the firebombing of Japan, focusing on planning, targets, forces, and operational results, rather than close air support for ground troops or artillery bombardment.

anchors.name: D-Day and the Normandy landings
anchors.definition: The chunk is substantially about the Allied invasion of Normandy (June 1944) as the opening of a second front in Western Europe, including its operational objectives, the strategic planning and breakdown of the landings, intelligence support specific to the invasion (French Resistance assistance to the Allies, the deception operation that led the Germans to expect an attack at Calais), Stalin’s interest in the second front as it relates to the invasion, and the results of the landings.

anchors.name: Appeasement of Germany in the 1930s
anchors.definition: This chunk is substantially focused on the policy of appeasement adopted by the future Allies towards Hitler’s efforts to flout the Versailles Treaty with rearmament and treaty renegotiation, a desire for Lebensraum, and aggressive actions taken towards countries such as Austria, Czechoslovakia, etc.

anchors.name: Munich Agreement and Czechoslovakia
anchors.definition: This chunk is substantially about the Sudeten crisis and the 1938 Munich conference, including the individuals involved as they pertain to the conference (Chamberlain, Hitler, Daladier, Mussolini, and Czechoslovak leaders such as Beneš), up to Chamberlain’s “peace in our time” statement, focusing on the events and the Czechoslovak situation rather than the broader policy of appeasement toward Germany.

anchors.name: Nazi-Soviet Pact (Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact) and its fallout
anchors.definition: This chunk is substantially about the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, Hitler’s uneasy non-aggression pact with Stalin that shocked the West, and its fallout: the implications for Poland, the Soviet takeover of the Baltic states, the Winter War with Finland, and the launch of Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Focus on where the passage connects those events to the pact.

anchors.name: US shift from neutrality to intervention
anchors.definition: This chunk is substantially focused on the U.S.’s initial refusal to become entangled in European affairs, F.D.R.’s campaign on that promise, but the U.S. increasingly seeing the Presidency go against Congress’s explicit resolve to stay neutral and steadily promising more support to the Allies, through identifying loopholes in the Neutrality Act. Its pursuit of Lend-Lease as it pertains to the U.S.’s abandonment of total neutrality, and eventually its declaration of war on not just Japan, but Germany and Italy in response to Hitler’s and Mussolini’s declarations of war on the U.S.
